walkthroughs.body_html:
Energy hides in stores. ⚡

You need to know eight: kinetic (moving), gravitational (raised up), elastic (stretched/squashed), chemical (bonds), thermal (hot stuff), magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear.

A store is where the energy is — not how it moves.

Energy can move between stores in four ways:

mechanically (a force pushing), electrically (a current), by heating, or by radiation (light or sound).

Example: a kettle transfers energy electrically from the mains to its thermal store of water.

Energy can't be created or destroyed.

It just shifts from one store to another. A falling ball loses gravitational energy and gains kinetic energy — the total stays the same.

Some energy is often dissipated (spread out as heat or sound), but it's still there.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT one of the energy stores?
options: Kinetic
Joule
Elastic
Chemical

mcqs.q: A torch is switched on. Energy is transferred from the chemical store of the battery mainly by…
options: Heating
Radiation (light)
Sound waves
Gravity

mcqs.q: When energy is 'lost' as heat due to friction, what has really happened?
options: Energy has been converted into mass following E=mc^2.
Energy has been used up and no longer exists.
Energy has been transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings — it's not destroyed, just dissipated.
Efficiency above 100 percent is possible if the device extracts ambient energy.

mcqs.q: If a car doubles its speed, what happens to its kinetic energy?
options: Kinetic energy doubles because energy is proportional to speed.
Energy has been converted into mass following E=mc^2.
It quadruples (because KE = 1/2 mv^2 — kinetic energy is proportional to v^2).
Kinetic energy stays the same because mass hasn't changed.

mcqs.q: Can a device ever be 100 percent efficient?
options: Efficiency above 100 percent is possible if the device extracts ambient energy.
Energy has been converted into mass following E=mc^2.
In practice, no — some energy is always transferred to less useful stores (e.g. heat to surroundings).
A well-designed device can be 100 percent efficient by eliminating all friction.
